questions.prompt: With Kotlin's context parameters (introduced in Kotlin 2.2), you declare `context(logger: Logger) fun sync() { ... }`. How is `sync()` called, and how does its body use the logger?

choices.text: The caller passes it as `sync(logger)`, and the body calls `log()` bare
The caller needs a `Logger` in context; the body calls `logger.log()`
Any caller works, since Kotlin injects a `Logger` from the DI graph
The caller needs a `Logger` in context; the body calls `log()` bare

questions.explanation: Context parameters are resolved implicitly at the call site from a matching value in the caller's context, for example inside `context(logger) { sync() }` or another function with a `Logger` context. Unlike the older context receivers, they are not receivers in the body, so you use their name: `logger.log(...)`. Nothing comes from a DI framework, and they aren't passed like ordinary arguments.

sources.title: Context parameters
sources.claim: Context parameters are declared with `context(name: Type)` and resolved implicitly from a matching value in the caller's scope, with an ambiguity error if several match; constructors can't declare them, and properties with them can't have backing fields, initializers or delegation.

sources.title: What's new in Kotlin 2.2.0
sources.claim: Kotlin 2.2.0 introduces context parameters, which replace context receivers; they are not receivers in the function body, so you access their members by the parameter's name.

questions.prompt: Following the layering in Android's guide to app architecture, which of these dependencies points the wrong way?

choices.text: A use case that depends on `NewsRepository` and `AuthorsRepository`
A ViewModel that uses `NewsRepository` directly, with no use case
A repository that calls `FormatDateUseCase` from the domain layer
A use case that depends on another use case, `FormatDateUseCase`

questions.explanation: In the guide, the UI layer depends on the optional domain layer, and the domain layer depends on the data layer: use cases usually depend on repositories, and may depend on other use cases. The data layer depends on neither, so a repository calling a use case reverses the arrow. A ViewModel may still use a repository directly: the guide adds use cases only when they are needed.

sources.title: Guide to app architecture
sources.claim: The arrows in the guide's diagrams represent dependencies between classes; the domain layer depends on data layer classes and, when included, provides dependencies to the UI layer.

sources.title: Domain layer
sources.claim: Use case classes usually depend on repository classes and can depend on other use cases, and the UI layer may still access repositories directly; use cases are added only when required.

questions.prompt: Your Hilt instrumented tests must use `FakeAnalyticsService` instead of the real binding in `AnalyticsModule`. Compare `@TestInstallIn`, `@UninstallModules` and `@BindValue`, and say which you would use by default.

model_answer.summary: Default to a `@TestInstallIn` module that replaces `AnalyticsModule` for every test in the folder; use `@UninstallModules`, with a nested module or a `@BindValue` field, only for a single test class that needs something different, because it creates new components and slows builds.
key_points: `@TestInstallIn(components = [...], replaces = [AnalyticsModule::class])` on a module in the test or androidTest folder replaces the binding for all tests in that folder, and is the recommended option whenever possible

`@UninstallModules(AnalyticsModule::class)` with a nested `@InstallIn` module replaces the binding for one test class only, and Hilt creates new components for such tests, which can significantly increase build times
`@BindValue` on a test field binds it into the graph under its type and qualifiers, so a test can replace and reference the fake (or a mock) in one place
`@UninstallModules` can only remove `@InstallIn` modules, not `@TestInstallIn` ones or modules without `@InstallIn`

questions.explanation: The options trade scope against cost: a shared `@TestInstallIn` replacement keeps one set of components for all tests, while per-class replacement is flexible but makes Hilt generate more. Plain unit tests usually don't need Hilt at all: construct the class with fakes.

sources.title: Hilt testing guide
sources.claim: A `@TestInstallIn` module in the test or androidTest folder replaces a binding for all tests in that folder and is recommended whenever possible; `@UninstallModules` replaces it for one test class, can only uninstall `@InstallIn` modules, and makes Hilt create new components that can significantly impact build times; `@BindValue` binds a test field under its type and qualifiers.

retired.reason: Written Questions are legacy (ADR-0008): replaced by a multiple-select Question on the same Concept.

questions.prompt: Which of these declarations with a Kotlin context parameter `context(u: Users)` is allowed?

choices.text: A property with an initializer, such as `val cache = u.loadAll()`
A property delegated with `by lazy` that reads the parameter `u`
A getter-only property, such as `val first get() = u.first()`
A class's primary constructor that declares `context(u: Users)`

questions.explanation: Properties with context parameters can't have backing fields, initializers or delegation, so only a getter-only property works: the getter reads `u` each time it is called. Constructors can't declare context parameters at all.

sources.title: Context parameters
sources.claim: Constructors can't declare context parameters, and properties with context parameters can't have backing fields, initializers or delegation; a context property is written with a getter, such as `context(users: UserService) val firstUser: String get() = users.findUserById(1)`.

questions.prompt: A `GetPaymentsUseCase` in the domain layer needs payment data from the server and the local cache. What should it depend on?

choices.text: `PaymentsRepository`, the data layer's entry point for payment data
`PaymentsApi`, the Retrofit data source, to skip one extra layer
`PaymentsViewModel`, since it already holds the screen's loaded data
`PaymentsDao` and `PaymentsApi`, merged together in the use case

questions.explanation: Use cases depend on repositories, and repositories are always the entry points to the data layer: use cases and state holders should never take a data source such as a Retrofit API or a DAO as a direct dependency. Depending on a ViewModel would point from the domain layer back up to the UI layer.

sources.title: Data layer
sources.claim: Other layers should never access data sources directly; the entry points to the data layer are always the repository classes, and state holders or use cases should never have a data source as a direct dependency.

sources.title: Domain layer
sources.claim: Use case classes usually depend on repository classes from the data layer.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Hilt's `@UninstallModules` is true, according to the Hilt testing guide?

choices.text: It can uninstall a `@TestInstallIn` module for one single test class
It applies to all tests in the folder, the same way `@TestInstallIn` does
Hilt builds new components for its tests, which can slow test builds
It can remove any Dagger module, including ones without `@InstallIn`

questions.explanation: Hilt creates new components for tests that use `@UninstallModules`, which can significantly impact build times, so the guide prefers `@TestInstallIn` when a binding must be replaced in all test classes. `@UninstallModules` affects only the annotated test class, and it can uninstall only `@InstallIn` modules: naming a `@TestInstallIn` module or one without `@InstallIn` is a compile error.

sources.title: Hilt testing guide
sources.claim: `@UninstallModules` replaces a binding for a single test class, can only uninstall `@InstallIn` modules (not `@TestInstallIn` ones, and not modules without `@InstallIn`, which is a compilation error), and because Hilt creates new components for those tests it can significantly impact build times.

questions.prompt: Your Hilt instrumented tests must use `FakeAnalyticsService` instead of the real binding in `AnalyticsModule`. Which statements match the Hilt testing guide? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A `@TestInstallIn` module in `androidTest` replaces it for every test there
`@UninstallModules` can also remove a module annotated `@TestInstallIn`
`@TestInstallIn` is the recommended option whenever it is possible
`@UninstallModules` makes Hilt build new components, which can slow builds
`@BindValue` works only with plain fakes, so it can't bind a Mockito mock

questions.explanation: A `@TestInstallIn` module with `replaces = [AnalyticsModule::class]` in the test or androidTest folder replaces the binding for every test in that folder, and the guide recommends it whenever possible. `@UninstallModules` replaces it for one test class, but Hilt then generates new components for that test, which can significantly impact build times, and it can only uninstall `@InstallIn` modules, not `@TestInstallIn` ones. `@BindValue` binds a test field under its type and qualifiers, and the guide shows it on a Mockito `@Mock` field too.

sources.title: Hilt testing guide
sources.claim: A `@TestInstallIn` module replaces a binding for all tests in the test or androidTest folder and is recommended whenever possible; `@UninstallModules` replaces it for one test class, can only uninstall `@InstallIn` modules, and makes Hilt create new components that can significantly impact build times; `@BindValue` binds a test field, including a Mockito mock, under its type and qualifiers.
